name: Antigua and Barbuda
rule: Supported by a combined domestic-category and commodity-classification inference for the stated manufactured plain tea. The PPU’s 27 August 2020 all-country commodity table applies permit/phytosanitary requirements to Categories 2–4. Its signed 17 June 2021 guidance and current website require documents for regulated plant commodities and describe processed items that still carry pests; the PPU expressly operates within IPPC standards. Current-linked ISPM 32 section 2 and Appendix 2 identify tea as a Category 1 example. This is a reasoned application of the domestic scheme, not a freestanding international exemption. A broad older leaflet requiring certificates for non-regulated items was recovered in an IPPC report dated 14 May 2014; the ministry copy uploaded in 2022 changes only its contact email. Newer signed/current guidance supplies the operative narrower scope. Separate enacted food laws reviewed do not impose a blanket private-tea origin certificate.
personalMailApplicability: Product-scope inference applies to a clean sealed 100 g manufactured Camellia tea packet bought for personal use and sent by post; it is not a traveler or gift allowance. Ordinary customs declaration and arrival inspection remain.
authority: Antigua and Barbuda Plant Protection Unit
researchAttempts: Reviewed PPU import guidance and the 27 August 2020 commodity-status table, including processed-food examples. No explicit heat-processed Camellia tea classification or small postal waiver found.

2026-09-30: Re-read the current official PPU page in the browser. It regulates any quantity only when the article is regulated; processing examples include crushed herbs, dehydrated fruit/vegetables and other pest-bearing preparations, but do not classify steamed manufactured Camellia tea. No published product determination found; did not infer either automatic exemption or a Japan-origin ban.

Read official Public Health Act Cap. 353, Part VI: section 49 defines food and importer broadly; section 57(1)(a) authorizes food-import regulations for food intended for sale; section 66(e) enforces applicable food-import regulations; section 67 permits sampling of imported consignments. These provisions do not themselves create a blanket origin/free-sale/health-certificate requirement for private tea imports.

Read official Importation Protection Act Cap. 211 sections 3–6: section 3 authorizes controls for imported articles intended for sale and contains a rebuttable sale presumption. The express origin-health-certificate duty in section 4 applies to secondhand clothing, not tea. The traveller personal-effects exception in section 6 likewise concerns clothing, so it was not used as a food exemption.

Searched official legislation, ministry health guidance, food-import requirements and free-sale certificate terms. The located Food Safety Act 2017 file is in the Bills collection and the ministry labels its 2020 text Food Safety Bill; neither was treated as an enacted private-import obligation. No separate enacted blanket food-certificate or import-approval rule was established. The existing plant-risk classification gap therefore remains unresolved.

30 September bounded legal-scope peer review: The operative public guidance consistently limits permits and certificates to regulated commodities. The complete table addresses Categories 2–4; it is not a complete list of exempt Category 1 goods. Its examples include crushed herbs, dehydrated fruit/vegetables, and even a steam/pressure-treated tamarind commodity. These demonstrate that either being processed or having a heat treatment in the name does not automatically prove exemption. No table entry or local processing definition settles steamed/dried Camellia tea. Japan omission cannot itself be treated as a ban outside the regulated scope.

Re-read saved enacted Public Health Act sections 57/66 and Importation Protection Act sections 3–6: food-import regulation powers and sale scope do not themselves create an unqualified personal-tea foreign certificate duty; the express certificate provision concerns used clothing. No separate mandatory special food document was established for this private packet.

ANMAT3280/2025 removes the personal-food import authorization; the August2026 transfer of food supervision to SENASA does not reinstate it.
personalMailApplicability: Processing-based agricultural exemption applies to imports from third countries, including Japan, without restricting transport to baggage. Personal-food authorization repeal is for direct users and personal use. Normal postal/customs import procedures remain.

name: Aruba
rule: Tea is an economic-licence commodity, but article 1(2) of the current Landsbesluit invoervergunning goederen expressly exempts consignments with CIF value at most Afl.400, destined for natural persons and not imported for trade. DEACI food guidance requires sanitary certificates for perishables, and says no import certification documents are required for ordinary food; manufactured dry tea is a nonperishable food.
personalMailApplicability: The legal exemption is per consignment to a natural person for noncommercial use, with no traveler-only or gift-only wording. DEACI also addresses parcel-post/mail-order shipments. Apply only to sealed manufactured plain tea for the recipient’s own consumption.

quantityLimit.scope: CIF value per noncommercial consignment to a natural person, including freight and insurance; economic licence exemption, not a weight limit.

name: Barbados
rule: Plant Protection Act 2023–2, assented16 February 2023 and commenced29 May 2024 by SI 2024/23, replaces the previously cited Cap.268 (2007). Section 2 limits manufactured plant products to products whose nature/processing may create pest risk and section 2(2) expressly requires interpretation in accordance with ISPM 5. Sections 14 and18(4) require internationally harmonised, scientific/risk-based measures. The current-linked ISPM 32 Appendix 2 illustrates tea as Category 1; normative Category 1 guidance says processing has made the commodity incapable of carrying quarantine pests and no phytosanitary measures should be required for pests eliminated by that processing. Combining the domestic scope and mandatory standards interpretation with that actual tea example supports treating the stated factory-manufactured steamed/rolled/dried pure sencha as outside the Act’s plant-product/regulated-article document route. This is an explicit legal-scope inference, not a Barbados tea-specific ruling; Appendix 2 itself is reference-only/non-prescriptive. Sections 18–20 permit, certificate and advance-notice duties attach to covered articles. Independent Food Hygiene Regulations 26A allows arrival inspection and discretionary requests for an origin inspection certificate but does not impose a universal advance foreign certificate. A domestic wholesome-food certificate issued following inspection is not a certificate the volunteer exporter must procure.
personalMailApplicability: Section 27 expressly covers postal and courier interception of regulated articles. The inference concerns statutory manufactured-product scope and is therefore not limited to travellers or gifts: it covers the stated paid personal postal sencha. Ordinary declaration, inspection, uncontaminated packaging and compliance with any actual pest finding remain necessary.
authority: Barbados Government Printing Department / Plant Protection Organization / Ministry of Health; IPPC current-linked ISPM 32 for commodity interpretation
researchAttempts: Reviewed the government plant-import procedure and personal-consumption/mail form options. Searched operative tea processing exemptions; did not rely on a draft replacement Plant Protection Act.

name: Saint Barthélemy
rule: The current territorial Environment Code, consolidated after 12 March 2026, restricts living specimens under Article 32-17; its plant annex concerns living plants, fruiting bodies and propagules. The inherited national certificate schedules do not list finished tea; the unresolved issue is the separate local restriction. Organic Law 2007-223 Article 18 IX preserves applicable pre-2007 provisions and substitutes the new territorial references. This supplies a continuity basis for inherited national schedules, whose finished-tea list-based treatment does not itself require a new tea-specific ruling. Current Code rural expressly adopts a risk-qualified manufactured-product definition. Its statutory2020commencement conflicts with current Ministry2026-165 guidance retaining the older framework; neither claim is omitted. This does not establish a tea prohibition.

name: Bonaire, Saba and Sint Eustatius
rule: The official current BES Invoeringswet, article 18.2.4a(c)–(d), limits plants to living plants/parts and plant products to unprocessed products or products subjected only to simple processing. Article 18.2.4b authorises import conditions within that scope; it does not itself impose a certificate on every plant-derived food. The described steamed, repeatedly rolled/pressed, hot-air dried sencha is a finished manufactured food, with ISPM32 Category 1 tea providing technical corroboration. The better general-category inference places it beyond simple processing and therefore outside that plant-product control class. This applies the BES statute itself, which covers Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, rather than importing European Netherlands rules or extending Bonaire’s Venezuela-only notice. The statutory used-packaging category does not create a duty for clean new factory and postal packaging. No contrary applicable tea or broad manufactured-food condition was recovered in the bounded island/national rule check.
personalMailApplicability: This conclusion follows commodity scope in the applicable local law, not a baggage, gift or noncommercial-seller exception. It applies to the stated private direct postal purchase and clean new packaging.

name: Bahamas
rule: The 2024 plant-permit HS list omits 0902 tea, leaving the phytosanitary classification unverified. A separate recovered instrument, Import Control (Foods, Plants and Animals) Regulations 1993 (SI 50/1972 as amended SI 35/1993), regulation 4(1), requires a written agriculture-authority licence for any food import, without a business-only or personal-post limitation. No automatic exemption applicable to the stated ordinary sealed sencha packet was established. This conclusion relies on the separate food-import licence, not a phytosanitary certificate or section 35 of the business-scoped 2016 Food Act.
personalMailApplicability: Inference from an unqualified any-person/any-food import licence duty, independent of the 2016 Food Act business scope.
